description: Test your knowledge of Cranial nerve nuclei & Cerebral hemispheres.

cards.text: Name the 7 functional columns of cranial nerve nuclei and give one example cranial nerve for each.
cards.answer: GSA (CN V), GVA (CN X), SVA (CN VII), SSA (CN VIII), GSE (CN XII), GVE (CN III), SVE (CN V). Each column represents a functional category: sensory (afferent) or motor (efferent), applied to general or special structures.

tip.tip: Mnemonic: 'General & Special, Afferent & Efferent' — two dichotomies (general/special × sensory/motor)

cards.text: Which cranial nerves carry SVE (branchiomotor) fibers, and what muscles do they innervate?
cards.answer: CN V (mastication), CN VII (facial expression), CN IX (stylopharyngeus), CN X (pharyngeal/laryngeal muscles), CN XI (sternocleidomastoid/trapezius). SVE nuclei originate from the nucleus ambiguus.

tip.tip: SVE nerves = 5, 7, 9, 10, 11 (branchiomotor sequence); all innervate pharyngeal arch-derived muscles

cards.text: What is Broca's area, where is it located, and what type of aphasia results from its damage?
cards.answer: Brodmann areas 44 and 45, left inferior frontal gyrus (precentral region). Damage causes Broca's aphasia: non-fluent speech (halting, effortful), preserved comprehension, intact repetition usually spared.

tip.tip: Broca's = 'Broken speech' — patient struggles to speak but understands

cards.text: Describe the somatotopic organization of the primary motor cortex (area 4) and the clinical consequence of a focal central sulcus lesion.
cards.answer: Motor cortex organized medial-to-lateral: leg (medial, near falx) → trunk → arm → hand → face (lateral). Lesion causes contralateral weakness, most pronounced in the arm and face due to larger cortical representation.

tip.tip: 'Motor homunculus' — disproportionately large hands and face because fine movement requires more cortical space

cards.text: What cranial nerves carry taste sensation, which portion of tongue do they supply, and what nucleus processes this signal?
cards.answer: CN VII (anterior 2/3 tongue via chorda tympani), CN IX (posterior 1/3 via lingual branch), CN X (epiglottus). All three project to the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) in the medulla.

tip.tip: '7 anterior (2/3), 9 posterior (1/3)' — CN VII before the 'division line' at the sulcus terminalis; CN IX after

cards.text: Differentiate Broca's aphasia from Wernicke's aphasia: location, speech output, and comprehension.
cards.answer: Broca's: left inferior frontal (area 44/45), non-fluent/halting speech, comprehension preserved. Wernicke's: left superior temporal (area 22), fluent but meaningless (jargon), comprehension impaired. Patient with Wernicke's unaware of errors.

tip.tip: Broca's = 'Broken' (effort to speak); Wernicke's = 'Word salad' (fluent nonsense, poor understanding)

cards.text: Which nucleus in the medulla receives taste (SVA), visceral sensation (GVA), and general sensation (GSA) from cranial nerves VII, IX, and X?
cards.answer: Nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) in the medulla. It receives convergent input from CN VII (taste anterior 2/3 + viscera via vagus afferents), CN IX (taste posterior 1/3 + carotid body chemoreception), and CN X (taste epiglottis + thoracoabdominal viscera).

tip.tip: 'Solitarius = solitary tract' — where these sensory nuclei converge in the medulla; relay to parabrachial nucleus → thalamus

cards.text: What is the embryological distinction between GSE and SVE motor nuclei, and why does this matter clinically?
cards.answer: GSE nuclei innervate muscles derived from somites (extraocular muscles, tongue via CN XII), producing fine, graded, voluntary movement. SVE nuclei innervate muscles from pharyngeal arches (mastication, facial expression, pharynx), producing stronger, protective movements. Damage to each produces different motor deficits.

tip.tip: 'Somite = General; Pharyngeal arch = Special branchiomotor' — different embryological origins, different functional capabilities
